doc.title: Peter Vacher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

chapter: Joe Darensbourg and the Creole question
title: Reception of the Darensbourg book and the half-siblings' legal threat
summary: His widow was delighted; the half-siblings passing for white threatened legal action, so some names were omitted.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: What does his wife think of the book?

Yeah. Well it did justice to her Joe, because it came out just after he died unfortunately. He never saw the final thing. But it did justice in her views to Joe. She was proud as proud could be of her husband and a terrific booster of her husband, therefore this was the right and proper thing that should be done, and she never made any comments about it editorially. Well I’ll tell you what was most interesting about that, Joe is a Creole. He had two lots of brothers and sisters because his father married twice. And much of what I speak about in the early part of the book is about a Creole guy who, as he put it, covers both ways. That is to say he was a member of both the white and the black locals in Los Angeles, which is quite interesting, isn’t it? And he would work in Mexican bands, in white bands, in Creole bands, in black bands. And the real hassle we got was from the second lot of siblings, the half-brothers and half-sisters, all of whom were passing for white. And we had named their names in the original text. And I was threatened with a lawsuit by them unless I removed their names, because they were in a stage of their lives where they wanted no truck with someone who had appeared to be willing to live the

black lifestyle as Joe was. Because Joe didn’t give a damn about all that. So I was threatened. I don’t know how strongly or realistically, but I was threatened with some kind of legal action unless they were removed. Well I thought it wrong. You can’t deny that they existed. You can’t deny a whole part of Joe’s family. But we didn’t put names. You’ll find there’s a few names missing, a family who did not wish to be named.
